qs.q: For the copper current measurement, the cumulative distribution function of continuous random variable $X$ is given as: \[ F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x<0,\\ 0.05x, & 0\le x<20,\\ 1, & x\ge 20\end{cases} \] What is the probability density function of $X$?
hints: The density is the rate of change of the cumulative distribution function.
Differentiate each piece of $F$ separately.
$f(x)=\dfrac{dF(x)}{dx}$ wherever the derivative exists.

qs.q: Suppose that contamination particle size (in micrometers) can be modeled as \[ f(x)=\begin{cases}2x^{-3}, & x>1,\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases} \] Determine the mean of $X$.
hints: This is the mean of a continuous random variable given by its density.
Set up $\int x f(x)\,dx$ over the range where $f$ is non-zero.
$E(X)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x f(x)\,dx$.

qs.q: Suppose the current measurements in a strip of wire are assumed to follow a normal distribution with a mean of 10 milliamperes and a variance of 4 (milliamperes)$^2$. What is the probability that a measurement will exceed 13 milliamperes?
hints: This is a normal probability: standardise and use the standard normal table.
Compute the $z$-value of 13 using the standard deviation (the square root of the variance), then find the upper-tail area.
$Z=\dfrac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$ and $P(X>x)=1-\Phi\left(\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)$.
steps: $P(Z>1.5)=1-0.9332\approx0.0668$, which is closest to the choice 0.0681 (the printed key; table rounding).

qs.q: In a large corporate computer network, user log-ons to the system can be modeled as a Poisson process with a mean of 25 log-ons per hour. What is the probability that there are no log-ons in an interval of 6 minutes?
hints: Count the log-ons in a fixed interval: this is a Poisson count.
Convert the rate to the 6-minute interval first, then find the probability of zero log-ons.
If $N\sim\text{Poisson}(\lambda t)$ then $P(N=0)=e^{-\lambda t}$.
steps: Rate 25 per hour, so in 6 minutes (0.1 hour) the mean is $25(0.1)=2.5$.

qs.q: In a large corporate computer network, user log-ons to the system can be modeled as a Poisson process with a mean of 25 log-ons per hour. What is the interval of time (in minutes) such that the probability that no log-on occurs in this interval is 0.90? (Note: Interval refers to the length of time from start until first log-on)
hints: No log-on in an interval of length $x$ means the waiting time to the first log-on exceeds $x$: exponential distribution.
Convert the rate to log-ons per minute, then solve $P(X>x)=0.90$ for $x$.
For exponential with rate $\lambda$: $P(X>x)=e^{-\lambda x}$.

qs.q: In a large corporate computer network, user log-ons to the system can be modeled as a Poisson process with a mean of 25 log-ons per hour. What is the standard deviation of the time (in minutes) until the next log-on?
hints: The time until the next event in a Poisson process is exponential.
Express the rate per minute, then use the exponential standard deviation.
Exponential($\lambda$): $\mu=1/\lambda$ and $\sigma=1/\lambda$.

qs.q: The time to failure (in hours) of a bearing in a mechanical shaft is satisfactorily modeled as a Weibull random variable with $\beta=\frac12$ and $\delta=5000$ hours. What is the mean time (in hours) until failure?
hints: This is the mean of a Weibull distribution, which involves the gamma function.
Compute $1+1/\beta$ and evaluate the gamma function there.
Weibull mean: $\mu=\delta\,\Gamma\left(1+\dfrac1\beta\right)$, and $\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!$ for integers.

qs.q: The lifetime of a semiconductor laser has a lognormal distribution with $\theta=10$ hours and $\omega=1.5$ hours. What lifetime is exceeded by 99$\%$ of lasers?
hints: A lognormal variable has a normal logarithm, so work with $\ln X$ and a normal percentile.
Exceeded by 99$\%$ means 1$\%$ lie below, so find the $z$-value with area 0.01 to its left, then undo the logarithm.
$P(X<x)=\Phi\left(\dfrac{\ln x-\theta}{\omega}\right)$, so $x=\exp(\theta+z\,\omega)$.

qs.q: An electronics company manufactures resistors that have a mean resistance of 100 ohms and a standard deviation of 10 ohms. The distribution of resistance is normal. Find the probability that a random sample of $n=25$ resistors will have an average resistance less than 95 ohms.
hints: The population is normal, so the sample mean is exactly normal.
Find the standard error of the mean, then standardise 95.
$\bar X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)$, so $Z=\dfrac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$.

qs.q: Suppose that the random variable $X$ has the continuous distribution given by the following pdf: \[ f(x)=\begin{cases}1, & 0\le x\le 1,\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases} \] Suppose that a random sample of size $n=12$ is selected from this distribution. What is the sampling distribution of $\bar X$?
opts: The sampling distribution of $\bar X$ is approximately $N\left(\mu_{\bar x}=\frac12,\ \sigma_{\bar x}=\frac1{12}\right)$, by central limit theorem
The sampling distribution of $\bar X$ is exactly $N\left(\mu_{\bar x}=\frac12,\ \sigma_{\bar x}=\frac1{12}\right)$
The sampling distribution of $\bar X$ is approximately $N\left(\mu_{\bar x}=\frac12,\ \sigma_{\bar x}=\frac1{\sqrt{12}}\right)$, by central limit theorem
The sampling distribution of $\bar X$ is exactly $N\left(\mu_{\bar x}=\frac12,\ \sigma_{\bar x}=\frac1{\sqrt{12}}\right)$
The sampling distribution of $\bar X$ is approximately $N\left(\mu_{\bar x}=0,\ \sigma_{\bar x}=1\right)$, by central limit theorem
hints: The population is not normal, so the central limit theorem gives an approximate normal distribution for $\bar X$.
Find the mean and variance of one observation from this density, then divide the variance by $n$.
$\mu_{\bar x}=\mu$ and $\sigma_{\bar x}=\sigma/\sqrt n$; use $\mu=\int xf(x)dx$ and $\sigma^2=\int x^2f(x)dx-\mu^2$.
steps: The parent is not normal, so $\bar X$ is only approximately normal (CLT): $N\left(\frac12,\frac1{12}\right)$.

qs.q: A civil engineer is analyzing the compressive strength of concrete. Compressive strength is normally distributed with $\sigma^2=1000\,(\text{psi})^2$. A random sample of 12 specimens has a mean compressive strength of $\bar x=3250$ psi. It is desired to estimate the compressive strength with an error that is less than 15 psi at 99$\%$ confidence. What sample size is required?
hints: This is a sample-size problem for a mean with known $\sigma$.
The error is the margin of error; use the $z$ value for 99$\%$ confidence, solve for $n$ and round up.
$E=z_{\alpha/2}\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$, so $n=\left(\dfrac{z_{\alpha/2}\sigma}{E}\right)^2$, rounded up.

qs.q: The brightness of a television picture tube can be evaluated by measuring the amount of current required to achieve a particular brightness level. A sample of 10 tubes results in $\bar x=317.2$ and $s=15.7$. Find (in microamps) a 99$\%$ confidence interval on mean current required. What is the length of the resulting interval?
hints: $\sigma$ is unknown, so use a $t$ interval for the mean.
The length is twice the margin of error; find $t$ with $n-1=9$ degrees of freedom at 99$\%$ confidence.
Length $=2\,t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\dfrac{s}{\sqrt n}$.

qs.q: In a random sample of 85 automobile engine crankshaft bearings, 10 have a surface finish that is rougher than the specifications allow. How large a sample is required if we want to be at least 95$\%$ confident that our estimate $\hat p$ of the true proportion $p$ was within 0.05 regardless of the value $p$?
hints: This is a sample-size problem for a proportion where $p$ is not assumed known.
Regardless of $p$ means using the worst case for $p(1-p)$.
$n=\left(\dfrac{z_{\alpha/2}}{E}\right)^2p(1-p)$, with the maximum of $p(1-p)$ equal to 0.25; round up.

qs.q: Of 1500 randomly selected cases of lung cancer, 850 resulted in death within 10 years. Calculate a 95$\%$ two-sided confidence interval on the death rate from lung cancer. What is the upper limit of the resulting confidence interval?
hints: This is a large-sample confidence interval for a proportion.
Compute $\hat p$ from the counts, then its standard error, and add the margin to $\hat p$.
Upper limit $=\hat p+z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}$.
